title: 'It was ... him or me,' officer says
article: Const. Ira Macumber remains "tormented" by the shooting death of Deng Fermino Kuol, but the officer told a
fatality inquiry Friday he doesn't regret putting his gun to the man's neck and twice pulling the trigger.
The decision, said Macumber, ended what he described as a life and death struggle with the man who had just stabbed him in the arm and was bent on doing more.
"I've considered his life daily. At the time, it was either him or me," Macumber said, occasionally stopping to compose himself.
"He forced me to make that decision to take his life. It was crystal clear to me that it was life or death."
Macumber was working alone on the evening of Oct. 25, 2003, when he responded to a call at an apartment building.
Inside, Kuol was passed out drunk at the bottom of the staircase.
Macumber spoke to the residents who called to have the Sudanese immigrant removed from the building, telling them to go to bed and he would take care of the situation.
Macumber said he knew Kuol was intoxicated but there was no indication he was carrying a weapon.
But moments later, as the two attempted to make it up the stairs, Macumber said the situation turned violent.
He testified Kuol, 34, swung around to face him on the stairs.
He lunged at the officer, stabbing at his chest. Macumber's body armour deflected the knife, leading Kuol to stab him in the arm.
The pair fell down on the stairs and continued to struggle.
"I realized I was going to die if I didn't stop him," said Macumber.
The officer was able to trap the knife and Kuol's hand under his armpit, continuing to wrestle to subdue him.
"I yelled at him several times and I yelled 'Help,' " said Macumber. "I knew his intent was to retrieve the knife."
Macumber said his only option was to reach down to his right side and pull out his gun. As he brought the weapon to Kuol's chin, the weapon misfired.
"I pulled the trigger but it didn't fire," he said. "I brought the gun back down and ejected the round."
He then tried again.
"I fired two rounds -- it sounded like pop, pop," he said. "I didn't ever see any blood so I laid there."
Shaking, Macumber was able to call for help over the police radio. He also knew his pregnant wife, a Calgary Police Service dispatcher, was working and would hear the call.
"I said, 'I've been stabbed, Code 200 (officer in trouble), offender down,' " he recalled. "I heard a noise so I dove on him. I thought he was still alive."
Macumber's wound turned out to be superficial -- the knife slashed through three layers of his clothing.
"If I didn't have the jacket on ... it would have cut my bicep right off," he said.

Asked if he could have used any other use of force to restrain Kuol, Macumber said he "did the right thing." Pepper spray and his collapsible baton were not readily available, nor were they an option, he said.
"Over the last while I've done a lot of coulda', woulda', shoulda'," he told the inquiry. "He pulled a knife and stabbed me. I think I did my job."
Southern Alberta's assistant chief medical examiner, Craig Litwin, testified Friday that Kuol died as a result of the gunshot wounds. Two bullets were removed from Kuol's head.
Litwin said he noticed gunpowder residue on Kuol's neck which would indicate he was shot at close range.
Kuol also had a minor cut near his right eye and a small tear to his lower lip.
The only other injury, Litwin said, was a soft-tissue injury to Kuol's left wrist -- the same wrist Macumber was restraining during the struggle.
Toxicology tests done after Kuol's death showed he had a blood- alcohol level of more than four times the legal limit.
"Overall, this is a very high level of alcohol found," Litwin said. "Certainly, alcohol has the potential to make people angry and mad -- a so-called mean drunk."
Macumber said had he known of Kuol's past, which included several convictions for assault, or that the man was carrying a weapon, he would have handled the situation differently.
"I didn't have sufficient information in a timely manner before I got to this residence," he said. "I'm aware of what could have been done and what was done."
The fatality inquiry continues in provincial court Monday.
